key_findings.correction: Note: 'Both grey-matter comparisons use the same control group, so a chance difference in the controls would appear in both and be counted as shared (editors' reasoning). The familiality test does not guard against this: it asks whether a measure is more alike within true sibling pairs than within random pairs, which any measure that runs in families can pass whatever the controls' values; that the amygdala failed it shows only weaker within-pair resemblance for that cluster.'
key_findings.note: The finding is confirmed (SOM pp. 4–5: η = 1 error cluster per image, P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ and 8 × 10⁻⁴, four and eight clusters, intersection in three regions, single-sex comparisons; 145 participants, TFCE, 5000 permutations, corrected P < 0.05, thresholded skeleton means and the atlas regions of interest exported to SPSS). The note's second sentence draws a wrong inference: the familiality statistic (SOM p. 5) does not involve the controls, so it cannot show that the siblings' shared difference from them is not a chance feature of the control group.

missed: The supplement treats the amygdala as a familial marker in two places: its text names the putamen, amygdala/hippocampus and superior temporal gyrus/posterior insula as vulnerability markers for developing dependence (SOM p. 5), and the Fig. S2B legend calls the left amygdala and putamen an endophenotype effect (SOM p. 7). The main report says the amygdala enlargement failed the familiality test (P = 0.144) and may reflect non-familial factors (p. 603). This internal inconsistency belongs among the reporting issues and in the interpretation gap.

The familiality test measures how alike each measure is within families, not whether the group difference is shared. A measure that runs in families in everyone can pass it whether or not the siblings' difference from the controls is real; the report itself says brain structure is to a large extent inherited (p. 602). So 'familial' here means that the measure is alike within sibling pairs; the test cannot by itself show that the abnormality is shared. This bears on key finding 16's note and on how the claim words its familiality sentence.

Table S1's DAST-20 comparison (F 12.6, P 0.001) shows that the non-dependent siblings scored higher than the controls (0.5 against 0.0), although both are very low; the supplement's text calls both groups' drug experience minor. exposure.polysubstance and comparison.controls_other_drug_use give the means without saying that they differ.

The third shared cluster carries several labels: postcentral gyrus (Table S2; SOM p. 6 text), superior temporal gyrus/posterior insula (SOM p. 5 text; Table S3), postcentral gyrus, insula and superior temporal gyrus (Figs. 2C and S1), and posterior insula for its familiality test (p. 603). Minor; one line would keep readers from taking these for different clusters.
Fig. S1's legend speaks of grey-matter density, while the report and Table S2 speak of volume (modulated VBM, SOM p. 4). Minor.
